name: Auditing Smart Contracts
title: Auditing Smart Contracts
answer: Auditing smart contracts means reviewing the code that runs on a blockchain to check that it does what its authors claim and nothing more. The work covers token contracts, lending pools, bridges, governance modules and the automated payment logic that sits behind them. It sits inside digital asset accounting because a flaw in that code is a financial exposure, not only a software defect, and the auditor has to connect the two. The scope also includes the off chain parts that feed the contract, such as price oracles and admin keys, since those can change the contract's behaviour without touching its code.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Auditing smart contracts means reviewing the code that runs on a blockchain to check that it does what its authors claim and nothing more. The work covers token contracts, lending pools, bridges, governance modules and the automated payment logic that sits behind them. It sits inside digital asset accounting because a flaw in that code is a financial exposure, not only a software defect, and the auditor has to connect the two. The scope also includes the off chain parts that feed the contract, such as price oracles and admin keys, since those can change the contract's behaviour without touching its code.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The auditor works against a specific chain and a specific deployed address, using a block explorer to read the verified source and the transaction history. Standard tooling includes static analysers such as Slither, fuzzers such as Echidna, and formal verification tools, alongside a local fork of the chain for replaying real transactions. Test suites are written in the contract's own language, most often Solidity, and run against a simulated network before anything is tried on a live one. The evidence an auditor keeps is the commit hash, the compiler version and the exact bytecode that was deployed, because a contract can be changed after review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with reading the specification and the code side by side, then mapping every function that moves value or changes permissions. Auditors trace each path a user or an attacker could take, looking for reentrancy, unchecked return values, arithmetic errors, access control gaps and flawed upgrade logic. Findings are written up with a severity, a reproduction and a suggested fix, and the report is usually published after the team has responded. A second pass checks the fixes, and some engagements end in a formal verification step that proves specific properties hold for all inputs rather than for the cases someone thought to try.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: An audit report is a point in time opinion, not a guarantee, and the report itself should state which commit was reviewed and what was out of scope. Accounting and reporting teams rely on these reports as evidence of control, so the provenance of the report matters as much as its contents: who wrote it, when, and whether the reviewed code is the code now running. Where a contract holds client assets, the audit sits alongside custody, key management and disclosure obligations, and regulators increasingly expect the same record keeping as for any other financial system. The site tracks 229 compliance and regulation pages, which reflects how quickly the surrounding rules are still being written.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Coverage is moving from one off reviews toward continuous monitoring, with automated alerts when a deployed contract changes or an admin key is used. More of the checking is being done by machine, with AI assisted tools triaging findings so human reviewers spend their time on the logic that matters. Accountants are being drawn in earlier, not to read code but to confirm that what the contract does matches what the financial statements say it does. The open question is standardisation, since a report that satisfies one jurisdiction or one exchange may not satisfy the next.
